newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Forced Thai finance mergers seen positive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Forced Thai finance mergers seen positive.

text.p: In line with the old Thai saying that one rotten fish can spoil the whole basket, Thai authorities on Friday moved decisively to cut away the rot from the ailing finance sector.
Some analysts viewed the move as positive and overdue.

Others cautioned that the measures must be carefully implemented or existing problems, such as poor asset quality and non-performing loans, would linger and the Bank of Thailand could end up shouldering major burdens and open-ended costs.

"The investors will like it...The situation can't be sustained like this. Things had to be sorted out," said Irene Cheung, vice president of the corporate strategy and research group at Merrill Lynch.
"I hope we have seen the worst and the situation will improve further from here," she added.

Thai authorities on Friday ordered 16 financially-distressed firms to suspend operations for 30 days and to report plans to shape up within two weeks or have their licences revoked and be absorbed by bigger companies.
They also selected five major finance companies to lead the much-needed consolidation in the troubled sector and promised to give two to five banking licences to qualified parties.
The shape-up-or-ship-out message signified a drastic change in the Bank of Thailand's philosophy in handling financial crises.
In the past, the central bank fought tooth and nail to ensure finance companies' survival but now it has shown that it is prepared to bite the bullet and allow troubled companies to go under.

The government earlier this week issued decrees to relax the foreign equity participation in financial institutions which were in the past capped at 25 percent. The decrees also sought to smooth out the process of mergers and acquisitions.
The measures were meant to contain problems in the finance sector and stop them spilling over to the whole Thai economy which is now going through its worst crisis in over a decade.
The government said it expected the steps to restore confidence of investors in Thailand and therefore attract much-needed capital inflows to ease liquidity problems.
Thailand's beleaguered finance sector was hit hard after the economic bubble burst last year following a decade of boom.
It faces liquidity problems amid high interest rates and the quality of its assets is rapidly deteriorating due to overexposure to the glutted property sector.

"This is a good step and will accelerate the consolidation of the sector. Without the determined action plan, it will take a long time to happen...It also helps contain the problem," said Niwes Hemvachirakorn, a senior executive vice president at Nava Finance and Securities.
But the plan, although positive, could be more complex than most people anticipate and fails to solve the problem if not properly implemented, an analyst at a US investment bank noted.
With the non-performing loan problems escalating for the finance sector, it would be difficult to make decisions on who would shoulder the cost of bad assets.
In the purchase and assumption arrangement, acquiring companies purchase the deposits of the failed bank and assume responsibilities for most of the failed institutions' liabilities.
The arrangement could pose a dilemma for the Bank of Thailand, he said.

"If the Bank of Thailand is willing to shoulder most of the bad assets, then it will sweat when the bill comes...The Bank of Thailand does not know the real magnitude of non-performing loans. It might already be dealing with open-ended expense here," the US investment bank executive said.

"But if the central bank forces acquiring companies to shoulder most of the bad assets, then that won't solve the problem. Doubts will remain on asset quality, and so will risk and subsequently high cost of funds," he added.
